title: Reliability Rhythms Playbook for Feature Owners & Platform Partners
content:
Purpose
---
This playbook defines a lightweight, cross-functional operating rhythm to help feature teams (feature owners) and platform partners (SRE / platform engineering / observability) jointly own and iterate SLOs, runbooks, and operational tooling. It focuses on a pragmatic 90-day cadence to accelerate maturity without heavy process overhead.

Context & why this matters
---
- We’ve seen recurring incidents where SLO ownership and remediation steps were unclear between feature teams and platform services (e.g., KV-cache tier, routing fallbacks).
- Goal: reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) for customer-impacting degradations, align expectations on error budgets, and make SLO change decisions low-friction.

High-level objectives (90 days)
---
1) Establish a shared SLO template and lightweight review path so every feature has a measurable indicator and an owner.
2) Create a weekly "Reliability Rhythm" meeting + short async scoreboard to surface drift and defects.
3) Onboard 6 high-priority services to the new process (pilot group).
4) Produce 3 runbooks updated with platform-run escalation steps and a fallback policy.

Principles
---
- Keep it low ceremony: 30–45 minute recurring touchpoints, asynchronous scorecards.
- Clear separation of responsibilities: feature teams own intent/queries; platform owns telemetry, routing, and cluster-level mitigations.
- Small, tangible bets: each sprint pair (feature + platform) ships one observability or remediation improvement.
- Iterate the playbook with feedback from pilots; this document should be updated after the first 90-day cycle.

Roles & responsibilities (compact)
---
- Feature Owner (FO): defines customer-facing success criteria, owns SLO definition draft, first responder for functional causes.
- Platform Partner (PP): validates metric instrumentation, ensures alerting map to ops runbooks, owns cluster-level fallback policies.
- SRE Lead: coordinates cross-team prioritization, chairs weekly Reliability Rhythm, owns postmortem process.
- Observability Engineer: implements dashboards, creates golden queries, and maintains retention/cost tradeoffs.
- Release / Product Manager (optional): approves SLO changes that affect customers or contractual commitments.

90-day plan (phases)
---
Phase 0: Prep (week 0–2)
- Identify pilot services (target: 6). Capture current SLOs, owners, alerting, and runbooks.
- Create a shared workspace (confluence + scoreboard) and invite stakeholders.
- Kickoff: 45-minute alignment meeting with FOs + PPs + SRE Lead.

Phase 1: Define & Instrument (weeks 3–6)
- Each FO drafts SLO using the template below and marks required telemetry events.
- PP reviews and implements missing metrics (histograms, percentiles, availability counters).
- Observability Engineer delivers baseline dashboards and an error budget calculator.

Phase 2: Operate & Harden (weeks 7–11)
- Run weekly Reliability Rhythm meetings (30 min). Quick agenda: scoreboard review (5m), incidents & trends (10m), blockers (10m), action items (5m).
- Create or update runbooks with platform-level mitigation steps and rollback guidance.
- Implement one automation per service (example: automatic routing degrade to smaller model variant on latency spike).

Phase 3: Evaluate & Institutionalize (weeks 12–13)
- Run a mini-retro focused on signal quality, process friction, and tooling gaps.
- Update playbook and onboard next cohort.
- Produce a short summary for product leadership with recommended changes to SLAs or capacity planning.

Meeting rhythm & artifacts
---
- Weekly Reliability Rhythm (30 min, recurring): FO + PP + SRE Lead + Obs Eng. Outcome: updated action tracker.
- Monthly SLO review (60 min): expand attendees to PMs and Release. Outcome: approved SLO changes or rollout hold.
- Incident postmortem cadence: within 72 hours of Sev2/Sev1 incidents a short blameless triage note (1 pager) then full postmortem within 2 weeks.
- Asynchronous scoreboard: single-page doc with key signals (SLO burn rate, recent deploys, top failure modes).

SLO template (one paragraph plus fields)
---
Title: short, customer-facing
Objective sentence: e.g., "Keep request latency p95 under 250ms for READ endpoints serving authenticated traffic."
Metric: metric name and Prometheus-style query or trace-derived signal
Window: rolling 30-day / 7-day (pick appropriate)
Target: percentage or bound (e.g., 99.5% success)
Error budget policy: when to throttle rollouts / trigger emergency capacity
Owner: feature owner + backup owner
Tooling required: dashboard link, alert id, retention note
Change justification: short rationale and product impact

Runbook checklist (minimum viable)
---
- Top-level symptom description (1–2 lines).
- Quick triage steps (what to check in first 5 minutes).
- Platform mitigations (route-level, cache flush, circuit-breaker toggles).
- Escalation matrix (on-call -> SRE Lead -> Platform Eng).
- Postmortem and follow-up owners.

Decision rules (when to change an SLO)
---
- Do not change SLO to mask a regression.
- Consider change if: customer behaviour has shifted materially, product contract requires it, or the metric is noisy / unmeasurable and a reliable proxy exists.
- Approval path: FO proposes -> PP validates telemetry -> SRE Lead + PM signoff -> update scoreboard and change log.

Communications plan
---
- Short lived: use the Reliability Rhythm Slack channel for day-to-day alerts with threads for each service.
- Weekly summary: auto-post scoreboard snapshot to #reliability-weekly.
- Exec escalations: SRE Lead prepares a one-slide impact summary for Product Leadership within 24 hours for Sev1 incidents.

Instrumentation & tooling checklist
---
- Metric parity: at least one golden metric per customer journey (availability, latency, correctness).
- Distributed tracing enabled for the critical path with sampling configured for production.
- Dashboards: top-level SLO, burn-rate trend, top error causes, and recent deploy timeline.
- Alerting: action-oriented alerts (who should do what) with runbook link and severity.
- Cost guardrail: retention and cardinality guard to avoid runaway observability costs.

Pilot success criteria (for this 90-day run)
---
- 6 pilot services onboarded with SLOs and runbooks in place.
- Average time to mitigation (MTTM) for pilot cohort reduced by 30% vs last quarter.
- At least 3 platform automations deployed across pilots (routing fallback, cache warming, dynamic shard allocation).
- Playbook iterated and a plan for rollout to next 12 services created.

Risks & mitigations
---
- Risk: telemetry gaps delay onboarding. Mitigation: PP triage and a 2-week instrumentation focused sprint.
- Risk: feature teams overloaded. Mitigation: reduce FO scope to owner+backup and rely on platform runbooks.
- Risk: alert fatigue. Mitigation: triage and consolidate alerts during Phase 1; add suppressions for known noisy windows.

Quick start checklist for feature owners
---
1) Fill SLO template in two sentences.
2) Link to current dashboard + set up alert stub.
3) Book a 30-min review with your Platform Partner.
4) Identify one observable improvement you can ship in the sprint (e.g., histogram tagging, more precise query).

Notes / open questions
---
- How aggressive should default error budget burn policies be for early-stage products? (Discuss in week 2)
- Consensus on 30-day vs 7-day windows for bursty workloads needs to be tested.

Next steps (this week)
---
- SRE Lead to share pilot list and calendar invites for kickoff.
- Observability Engineer to seed a scoreboard document and example SLO template.
- Each prospective FO to draft a two-line SLO and post to the scoreboard before the kickoff.

Appendix: example scoreboard columns
---
- Service, SLO title, window, target, burn rate (24h), burn rate (7d), last deploy, owner, on-call, runbook link, outstanding actions

End of playbook (first draft)

This is intentionally concise — the goal is to get the pilots moving. We will expand runbooks and automation recipes during Phase 2. If this flows well, the playbook will be promoted from "in_review" to "final" after the pilot retro.
